context: All sequences run from bottom to top. A push adds an element at the top, and a pop removes and returns the top element.
description: Dashed squares show where elements were before an operation. They do not count as additional elements in the stack. A solid square moved outside the container shows the value returned by that pop.

steps.announcement: The initial stack is [1, 3, 2], with 2 at the top.
steps.explanation: The stack starts with three elements, [1, 3, 2] from bottom to top. The bottom is 1 and the top is 2. There is no return value.
steps.key_state: Initially, the stack is [1, 3, 2] from bottom to top, with 1 at the bottom and 2 at the top. There is no return value.
steps.title: Initial state

steps.explanation: The call push(5) adds 5 at the top. The existing elements keep their order. The stack now has four elements, [1, 3, 2, 5] from bottom to top, with 1 at the bottom and 5 at the top. The call returns no value.
steps.key_state: After push(5), the stack is [1, 3, 2, 5] from bottom to top, with 1 at the bottom and 5 at the top. There is no return value.
steps.title: push(5)

steps.explanation: The call push(4) places 4 on top of 5, making 4 the new top. The stack now has five elements, [1, 3, 2, 5, 4] from bottom to top, with 1 at the bottom and 4 at the top. The call returns no value.
steps.key_state: After push(4), the stack is [1, 3, 2, 5, 4] from bottom to top, with 1 at the bottom and 4 at the top. There is no return value.
steps.title: push(4)

steps.announcement: Pop and return the top element, 4. The new top is 5.
steps.explanation: The first call to pop() removes and returns the top element, 4. The element below it, 5, is on top again. The stack now has four elements, [1, 3, 2, 5] from bottom to top, with 1 at the bottom and 5 at the top. The returned 4 is outside the stack.
steps.key_state: After the first pop(), the stack is [1, 3, 2, 5] from bottom to top, with 1 at the bottom and 5 at the top. The call returns 4.
steps.title: First pop()

steps.announcement: Pop and return the top element, 5. The stack is back to [1, 3, 2].
steps.explanation: The second call to pop() removes and returns the top element, 5, leaving 2 on top again. The stack now has three elements, [1, 3, 2] from bottom to top, with 1 at the bottom and 2 at the top. The returned 5 is outside the stack.
steps.key_state: After the second pop(), the stack is [1, 3, 2] from bottom to top, with 1 at the bottom and 2 at the top. The call returns 5.
steps.title: Second pop()

prose.summary: Both pushes and pops happen at the top. The first element in is the last one out, or equivalently, the last one in is the first one out.
prose.title: Pushing and popping on a stack

context: All sequences run from bottom to top. A push adds an element at the top, and a pop removes and returns the top element.
description: Arrows connect five vertical panels from left to right, one for each row of the table below. The open upper end of each panel is the top of the stack, and the closed lower end is the bottom. Push arrows enter from above, and pop arrows leave through the top.
Dashed squares show where elements were before an operation. They do not count as additional elements in the stack. A solid square moved outside the container shows the value returned by that pop.

frames.explanation: First 5 is pushed, then 4 is pushed on top of 5. Only the top element can be popped, so 4 comes out first, then 5. The first one in is the last one out, or equivalently, the last one in is the first one out.
frames.title: Pushing and popping on a stack
